newsitem.title: JAPAN: New Japan administration leaves doubts over reform.
newsitem.headline: New Japan administration leaves doubts over reform.

text.p: The old-guard veterans in Japan's new cabinet look like an unlikely team to champion the reforms needed to ensure the economy flourishes in the 21st century, though pundits say they have the clout to succeed if they try.
Domestic corporations and overseas trading partners are keen to see Tokyo slash through the tangled red tape that stifles entrepreneurs, keeps costs high and hampers imports.
Many fear Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto and his Liberal Democratic Party (LDP) have little stomach for bold moves.
Hashimoto was re-elected on Thursday at the head of a new government in which the conservative LDP will rule on its own for the first time since it was booted out of power in 1993.

Instead of the formal coalition of his first term begun in January, the LDP -- which fell 12 seats shy of a majority in last month's election -- must rely on a loose link with two former ruling partners, who opted not to join the cabinet.
Hashimoto has been disturbingly silent on the subject of deregulation, loudly urged for the past three years by corporations, which fear suffocation under piles of red tape.

"Prime Minister Hashimoto has shown that he is keen on administrative reform, but he has said nothing at all about whether he is keen on deregulation," Atsushi Hama, an official at business lobby Keidanren, told Reuters.

Administrative reform -- a broad concept encompassing calls to restructure ministries to boost efficiency, cut the number of bureaucrats and give politicians greater control over policy -- was adopted as a key plank by politicians of nearly every ilk in the October 20 election.
But fearful of angering special interest groups, few spoke of deregulation on the campaign trail.
"Deregulation isn't even a buzzword anymore," said Robert Feldman, chief economist at Salomon Brothers Asia.

Hashimoto's new cabinet provides scant reassurance, dominated as it is by veteran LDP politicians, such as Finance Minister Hiroshi Mitsuzuka, trade chief Shinji Sato, and Chief Cabinet Secretary Seiroku Kajiyama.
"The cabinet...suggests that this is very much a standard LDP-type cabinet," Feldman said.

The cabinet does, however, include one outspoken proponent of reform -- 54-year-old Health Minister Junichiro Koizumi, who made waves when as post and telecommunications minister he suggested the privatisation of the postal service.

Hashimoto's silence has left many in the dark as to his real stance. "We Japanese don't know his real intention either," said Yoshio Suzuki, president of Asahi Research Centre and a member of a government advisory panel on deregulation.

The panel is working on a fresh set of proposals to be issued late this month or early next as the basis for the final update of a government deregulation plan to be adopted next March. "We have said it shouldn't stop there, but (Hashimoto) has said nothing on the subject," Keidanren's Hama said.
Still, some say that master politician Hashimoto, like many of the bureaucrats with whom he has close ties, is well aware of the need to forge ahead with deregulation.
"Deregulation is vital for the economy, and Hashimoto understands that," Asahi Research Institute's Suzuki said.
Hashimoto's old guard could in fact provide the knowledge and clout to accomplish change, while prospects of facing dissatisfied voters if they fail to act could serve as an incentive to do so.
"Administrative reform must include both deregulation and decentralisation, or else it is meaningless," said Toshiaki Kakimoto, managing director of the Japan Research Institute.
"If the LDP doesn't fulfil its promise to carry this out, it will suffer a huge defeat (in the next election) and I think Hashimoto is well aware of this," Kakimoto said.
Others say progress has been made in some areas and will continue, but worry the pace of reform will be too slow.

"The thing has really got going and probably will not stop. The only problem is whether there will be sufficient deregulation by 1998...or will it spill over into the next millennium," said Mike Makino, an American Chamber of Commerce in Japan member who sits on the government advisory panel.
"Will it be fast enough for the United States and other trading partners? I'm afraid the pace is probably a little too slow for them," he added.
